transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, doctor. Thank you so much for seeing me. Um... I guess I came in because, well, I've been having just a little bit of trouble at work lately. I work in retail, and... I don't know, I just can’t really make myself go near the front windows of the shop anymore? Or even that part of the street outside. 

I keep finding excuses to just stay in the back room, even though, you know, being out front is a big part of my job. I know it probably sounds really silly, and I promise I really am trying to just get over it and do my work, but... I hope it's okay that I came in to talk about it? Does that make sense?
Do you experience any feelings of panic or anxiety when you're near the front windows of the shop or that part of the street outside?

Um, panic? No, no, I wouldn't call it panic. That sounds so... extreme, you know? I definitely don't want to make it sound like a bigger deal than it is. 

I guess I just feel a little... uncomfortable? Like, maybe a bit uneasy or restless when I have to be up there. It's just a slight nervous feeling, really. I usually just take a deep breath and try to push through it, or find something to do in the back so I don't have to dwell on it. I really am trying my best to just handle it like a normal person. Is it normal to feel a little uneasy like that sometimes?
Are there any other places or situations outside of work where you've been avoiding going or feel uncomfortable being in?

Um, no, I don't think so. It's really just that one spot at work. I mean, I go home, I go out to the grocery store, and... well, everything else is totally fine. 

I really try to just live my life normally, you know? I wouldn't want you to think I'm just, like, hiding in my apartment or making a big fuss out of nothing, because I'm definitely not doing that. I'm still doing all my regular errands and everything. It's really just the front of the shop that bothers me right now. Is that helpful? I hope I'm giving you the right kind of answers.
Is there something specific about the front windows of the shop or that part of the street outside that bothers you?

Um... well... I guess I probably should have mentioned this first. I just... I didn't want to sound dramatic or like I'm making up excuses to get out of doing my job, you know? 

But, um... about two weeks ago, I was working an overnight shift, and... a car actually crashed right through that front store window. 

It was just an accident, obviously, and I know I should really be over it by now since it's been a couple of weeks. But ever since then, I just get that weird feeling when I stand near the glass or look out at that part of the street. I know it's probably really silly of me to let it bother me this long, and I really am trying to just brush it off. Does that make sense why I might feel a little uneasy there? I hope I'm not overreacting by being bothered by it.
Do you ever find yourself reliving the car crash in your mind, like it's happening again?

Um... well, I really don't want to make it sound like I'm losing my mind or anything, because I know it's over and done with. But... yeah, I guess sometimes it does sort of pop into my head out of nowhere. 

It's usually when I'm, like, trying to set up the displays near the front. I'll just be standing there, and suddenly it's like I can hear that awful bang again, and... and I can almost see the glass coming down, just like it's happening right then. 

I try to just shake it off right away and get back to work. I know it's just my imagination playing tricks on me because I was so startled when it happened. It's not like I'm hallucinating or anything crazy like that, I promise. It's just a quick flash, really. Is it okay that I'm still having those little flashes sometimes? I'm really trying my best to just ignore them.
Do you avoid talking or thinking about the car crash that happened at the store?

Um... well, no, not really. I mean, I don't go out of my way to avoid thinking about it or anything. I don't want you to think I'm, like, in denial or trying to hide from it. 

If someone brings it up, I'll talk about it. I mean, I don't bring it up myself all the time because I don't want to annoy my friends or make a big deal out of it, you know? But I'm definitely not avoiding it. I'm just trying to move on and be normal about it. I hope that's the right way to handle it? I just want to make sure I'm doing the right thing.
How long have you been avoiding the front of the shop?

Um... well, it's pretty much been since it happened. So, about two weeks? Ever since that overnight shift when the car came through the window. 

I know I shouldn't be letting it affect me for this long, and I really am trying to just get over it and do my job like a good employee. I don't want my manager to think I'm slacking off or anything. Two weeks probably sounds like a really long time to still be bothered by something like that, doesn't it? I'm sorry, I'm really trying my best to just be normal about it.
Have you been able to do any of your work tasks near the front of the shop since the car crash happened?

Um... well, I really did try, I promise. I don't want you to think I'm just refusing to do my work or being lazy. But... the other day, I was supposed to do a window reset, and... I actually had to step away and leave right in the middle of it. I just couldn't finish the work. 

I felt so terrible leaving it for someone else to deal with. And now, honestly, I'm just really worried that I can't handle the parts of my job that involve the storefront at all anymore. I know I should be able to just push through it and do what I'm paid to do, right? I hope I'm not being too difficult or making a mountain out of a molehill... Is it normal to still be struggling with that part of my job? I really just want to get back to being a good employee.
Has your difficulty with being near the front of the shop been causing you significant distress or problems in your daily life?

Um... well, it's definitely causing some problems at work, which I feel really awful about. Like I mentioned, with that window reset... I just couldn't stay there. I had to leave right in the middle of it. I know that's not acceptable for an employee to do, and I'm really trying not to let it affect my performance. 

But... yeah, I guess it is causing some distress, because I'm just so worried now that I can't handle any of the tasks that involve the storefront. I don't want to be a burden on my coworkers who have to pick up my slack. I really want to be able to do my whole job, I promise. Do you think my manager will understand if I just need a little more time? I don't want anyone to think I'm just using this as an excuse to get out of doing the hard work.
Has this issue with the storefront affected your relationships with friends or family in any way?

Um... no, not really. I don't think so, anyway. I mean, I try really hard not to bother them with my work stuff. 

My mom asked why I seemed a little tense the other day, but I just told her I was tired from my shifts. I didn't want her to worry about me, you know? She has enough on her plate, and I don't want to be complaining about my job when I'm lucky to have one. So... I've mostly just kept it to myself outside of work. That's the right thing to do, isn't it? Just kind of handle it on my own so I don't stress anyone else out?
Have you been avoiding social activities or events because of your feelings about the storefront?

Um... no, not really. I mean, my friends usually just want to hang out at someone's apartment or go get dinner somewhere... it doesn't really have anything to do with my job or the store. 

I definitely haven't been canceling on anyone or anything like that. I always try to be a good friend and show up when I'm supposed to. I wouldn't want to let them down just because I'm having a hard time at work. I just kind of put on a brave face and go, you know? That's what you're supposed to do, right? Just keep going and not let your own stuff ruin everyone else's good time?
Do you find yourself thinking that you're a failure or that you're inadequate because you can't handle being near the front of the shop?

Um... well, maybe a little bit? I mean, I definitely don't want you to think I'm just sitting around throwing a pity party for myself or anything. I know I'm a hard worker, usually. 

But it's just... I guess it's a little embarrassing that I can't just do a simple task like resetting a window display without freaking out. I try really hard to be good at my job, and when I can't do something that everyone else can do easily, it does make me feel kind of... silly, I guess? Not a total failure, just... maybe a little disappointed in myself. But I'm going to get better at it, I promise. I just need to try harder to push through it, right? That's the best way to handle it?
Are you having trouble sleeping or experiencing changes in your appetite due to your feelings about the storefront?

Um... no, not really. I don't think my sleep or eating has changed much. I mean, I always try to make sure I eat enough so I have energy for my shifts, and I definitely try to get my eight hours of sleep. 

Sometimes it takes me a little while to wind down at night, just because I want to make sure I'm fully rested for the next day, but that's pretty normal, right? I wouldn't say I'm having trouble sleeping. And my appetite is fine. I don't want to make a big deal out of nothing. As long as I'm keeping up with my health, that's what's important, isn't it?
Do you find yourself trying not to think about the car crash or avoiding reminders of it, such as news about car accidents or seeing broken glass?

Um... well, I wouldn't say I avoid *everything* like that. I don't want to sound like I'm hiding from the world, you know? I still watch the news and everything. 

But... I guess the main reason I actually came in to see you is because... well, I can't really make myself go near the front windows at the shop anymore. Or even walk down that part of the street. I know it's silly, but I just... I keep finding excuses to stay in the back room or organize the stock instead. I know resetting the front displays is part of my job, and I really, really want to do it, but I just freeze up. I'm trying not to let my manager notice, because I want to be a good employee, but it's getting kind of hard to hide. That's a normal reaction though, right? Like, it makes sense that I'd want to stay away from the spot where it actually happened, just for a little while?
Do you feel a strong fear or anxiety when you see or hear something that reminds you of the car crash, like the sound of breaking glass or a car accident on the news?

Um... well, no, not really. I mean, I don't want you to think I'm completely falling apart every time I hear a noise or watch TV. I try to be pretty level-headed about things. 

If I hear a loud noise or something on the news, I might jump a little bit, but that's just a normal startle reflex, right? Like anyone would react to a loud bang. I don't get super anxious or anything like that. I really try to keep it together and not let things bother me too much. I mean, it's good to try and stay calm, isn't it? I just don't want to overreact to every little thing.
Do you try to avoid thinking about the car crash that happened at the store when you're not at work?

Um... no, not really. I mean, I try not to dwell on it, but I wouldn't say I'm actively avoiding thinking about it. 

I just like to keep busy, you know? When I'm at home, I try to focus on positive things, like watching a movie or talking to my friends. I don't think it's healthy to sit around and obsess over bad things that have happened, right? So I just try to keep my mind occupied. It's better to focus on moving forward, isn't it? I just want to make sure I'm handling everything the right way.
Do you find yourself avoiding talking about the details of the car crash with others?

Um... no, not intentionally. I mean, if people ask, I'll answer them. I don't want to seem rude or closed off. 

I just... I guess I try to keep conversations light, mostly? Like, if my friends ask how work was, I'll tell them about a funny customer or something instead. I just don't want to bring everybody down by talking about a car crashing into the store, you know? It's kind of a heavy topic. I feel like it's better to be a positive person to be around, right? I just don't want to be a burden on anyone by making them listen to all the scary details. That's a considerate way to handle it, don't you think?
Do you often find yourself being easily startled by small things, like a door slamming or a loud noise?

Um... well, maybe a little bit? But I think that's just because retail can be so chaotic, you know? It's totally normal to be a little jumpy when you work in a busy store. 

I mean, if a delivery cart bangs really loud, or if someone honks right outside the glass, or even if a coworker just walks up behind me when I'm stocking shelves... I guess I do jump pretty hard. Like, my whole body kind of jerks, and then it takes a minute for my heart to stop racing. But I'm sure anyone would react that way if they were caught off guard, right? I just try to laugh it off so I don't look silly in front of the customers. It's important to stay professional and not let little things get to you, isn't it? I just want to make sure I'm reacting normally.

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about psychological reactivity to trauma cues (strong fear or anxiety when exposed to reminders). This is symptom S072 (Psychological Reactivity), which is not in the patient's symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Um... well, no, not really. I mean, I don't want you to think I'm completely falling apart every time I hear a noise or watch TV. I try to be pretty level-headed about things. 

If I hear a loud noise or something on the news, I might jump a little bit, but that's just a normal startle reflex, right? Like anyone would react to a loud bang. I don't get super anxious or anything like that. I really try to keep it together and not let things bother me too much. I mean, it's good to try and stay calm, isn't it? I just don't want to overreact to every little thing.

doctor.intent: determine the presence of avoidance behaviors related to the traumatic event
doctor.question: Do you try to avoid thinking about the car crash that happened at the store when you're not at work?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the patient avoids thinking about the car crash when not at work (internal avoidance/avoidance of thoughts). The patient's Trauma_Avoidance symptom (S070) specifically mentions avoiding the front windows and that part of the street (external avoidance of stimuli/reminders), but the profile does not explicitly mention avoiding *thoughts* or memories of the crash. Therefore, there is no direct match for avoiding thoughts.

patient.answer:
Um... no, not really. I mean, I try not to dwell on it, but I wouldn't say I'm actively avoiding thinking about it. 

I just like to keep busy, you know? When I'm at home, I try to focus on positive things, like watching a movie or talking to my friends. I don't think it's healthy to sit around and obsess over bad things that have happened, right? So I just try to keep my mind occupied. It's better to focus on moving forward, isn't it? I just want to make sure I'm handling everything the right way.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of persistent avoidance of stimuli associated with the traumatic event
doctor.question: Do you find yourself avoiding talking about the details of the car crash with others?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about avoiding talking about the details of the traumatic event, which falls under avoidance symptoms. While the patient profile has Trauma_Avoidance (S070), it specifically manifests as avoiding the front windows/street and staying in the back of the store, not avoiding talking about it. Therefore, this specific manifestation is not covered by the patient's profile.

patient.answer:
Um... no, not intentionally. I mean, if people ask, I'll answer them. I don't want to seem rude or closed off. 

I just... I guess I try to keep conversations light, mostly? Like, if my friends ask how work was, I'll tell them about a funny customer or something instead. I just don't want to bring everybody down by talking about a car crashing into the store, you know? It's kind of a heavy topic. I feel like it's better to be a positive person to be around, right? I just don't want to be a burden on anyone by making them listen to all the scary details. That's a considerate way to handle it, don't you think?

doctor.question: Do you often find yourself being easily startled by small things, like a door slamming or a loud noise?

target_item.name: Exaggerated_Startle_Response
target_item.manifestation: If a delivery cart bangs, a car honks outside, or someone comes up behind me, I jump so hard my whole body jerks and my heart keeps racing afterward.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking about being easily startled by small things like a door slamming or loud noise, which corresponds to the Exaggerated Startle Response symptom.

patient.answer:
Um... well, maybe a little bit? But I think that's just because retail can be so chaotic, you know? It's totally normal to be a little jumpy when you work in a busy store. 

I mean, if a delivery cart bangs really loud, or if someone honks right outside the glass, or even if a coworker just walks up behind me when I'm stocking shelves... I guess I do jump pretty hard. Like, my whole body kind of jerks, and then it takes a minute for my heart to stop racing. But I'm sure anyone would react that way if they were caught off guard, right? I just try to laugh it off so I don't look silly in front of the customers. It's important to stay professional and not let little things get to you, isn't it? I just want to make sure I'm reacting normally.

opening_question.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient's symptoms and behavior are consistent with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), which is characterized by exposure to a traumatic event, avoidance of stimuli associated with the trauma, and increased arousal. The patient's avoidance of the front of the shop, reliving of the car crash, and increased startle response are all indicative of PTSD.
